comparator.name: Media, Art, Design and Architecture
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from VU Amsterdam's current official sources for 2026-2027: the Media, Art, Design and Architecture curriculum overview page and the programme's 2026-2027 Teaching and Examination Regulations (TER/OER), including Article 10.2 (formal tracks/specialisations), Article 11 (curriculum structure), Article 12.1 (elective period) and Appendix 1 (the complete programme overview with course codes and EC weights for every track and every one of the four specialisations). Year 1 (60 EC) is common to all students regardless of specialisation and regardless of the Dutch-taught or English-taught track: ten compulsory 6-EC courses covering visual/material-culture analysis, European cultural history, the early modern/modern/contemporary history of media, art, design and architecture, academic and language skills, and research techniques, plus two zero-credit orientation modules and a zero-credit diagnostic language test that are not 180-EC components. At the end of year 1 every student chooses one of four formal specialisations named directly in the programme's own title and confirmed by TER Article 10.2: Media, Art, Design or Architecture. Year 2 (60 EC) combines five compulsory courses shared by every specialisation (Exhibition Machines, Historiography of Media, Art, Design and Architecture, Philosophy CIS-L&S-MKDA, World Heritage and Conflict, Urban Culture and Public Space) with five specialisation-specific compulsory courses. For the Media specialisation these are Film and Media History, Media Theory and Analysis, Mediating Environments, The Postmedium Condition: Contemporary Art and Media, and the Study Trip Media and Design. Year 3 (60 EC) opens with a genuinely open 30-EC elective period (TER Article 12.1: a minor, at least five individually chosen units of education with at least two at level 300, or a 12-EC internship plus three further units of education), followed by the compulsory shared courses Contesting Images and Current Debates in Art and Culture, the specialisation's Research Seminar (Research Seminar Media for this route), and the 12-EC BA-thesis MKDA with colloquium (TER Article 11.5). The registry's languages field records this normalized target as the Dutch-taught (NLD) offering; the Dutch-track course list in the OER programme overview for the Media specialisation is used, and its course names are given in their official English equivalents (OER Appendix 1 lists both the Dutch-track and the English-track year plans for every specialisation; the year 2 and year 3 course codes and EC weights are identical between the two tracks, and only a small number of year 1 course titles/codes are language-specific, e.g. Analyse van beeld en object / Image and Object Analysis, Onderzoekstechnieken / Research Methods, Academische vaardigheden: Kunst en Cultuur / Academic Skills Arts and Culture, Taaltoets NL / English Language Test). No further ambiguity remains: the OER programme overview establishes, for the Media specialisation, a complete and internally consistent 180-EC pathway with explicit EC weights and compulsory status for every component, so no OER article or further official source needed to be consulted beyond the curriculum overview and the OER itself.

Preserved as open space rather than instantiated with invented content.
Current Debates in Art and Culture
Bachelor's thesis and colloquium: an independent research project completed after all year 1 and year 2 (chosen specialisation) courses have been passed.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target cp-000106 is the generic Media, Art, Design and Architecture bachelor with no route/specialisation named in the registry. TER Article 10.2 confirms four formal, equally weighted specialisations available in the applicable academic year: Media, Art, Design and Architecture, one of which every student must choose at the end of year 1. Each specialisation contributes exactly the same 30 EC of year-2 specialisation-specific compulsory courses and the same 12-EC thesis/6-EC research-seminar structure in year 3, so none is formally larger, more advanced or more central within the curriculum than the others; the four fields are named together, in this order, in the programme's own title (Media, Kunst, Design en Architectuur) and are listed in the same order in TER Article 10.2. No official source (the curriculum overview, TER Article 10 objective/exit-qualifications text, or the specialisation descriptions) presents one specialisation as more representative of the programme's broad academic identity than the others; each is described only in terms of its own object of study. Because no route is clearly more representative and none is the least specialised (all four are equally specific, named specialisations rather than a generic/default option), the neutral tie-break in the route-selection rule applies: the official order in which the current curriculum names the specialisations is used, which selects Media, the first-listed specialisation. This selection was fixed before any UCR course was considered and does not depend on UCR fit.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: The general critical study of images, objects and spaces, and the historical roots of contemporary visual and material culture
The integrated study of media, art, design and architecture as interconnected fields of visual and material culture

Media studies as a formal graduation direction: the history, theory and analysis of film, television, internet and games in cultural context, including the post-medium condition of contemporary art and media
Digital media and the changing technologies of storytelling
Visual culture spanning painting to digital images
World heritage and cultural conflict; urban culture and public space
Philosophy and historiography of media, art, design and architecture
Contested images and visual politics; contemporary debates in art and culture
Independent research culminating in a bachelor's thesis in art and culture
adjacent: Art history and contemporary art (the Art graduation direction)
Design history and culture (the Design graduation direction)
Architecture, cities and spatial culture (the Architecture graduation direction)
questions: How do vacant or under-used urban buildings become creative hubs, and how does this reshape public culture?
How does contemporary gaming culture recycle and rework older visual-art and storytelling traditions?

trace: surveys western art from the early Renaissance to the present, tracing major stylistic movements and the impact of art institutions, markets, critics and historiographers, and introduces essential tools for visual analysis and interpretation, the general visual/material-culture and image/object-analysis foundation that year 1 requires of every specialisation

trains research design, descriptive and inferential statistics and quantitative reasoning, the shared academic research-methods and techniques training every specialisation requires in year 1 before independent thesis work
surveys the central questions and methods of Western philosophy from antiquity to the present, the shared philosophical-reflection component every specialisation carries in year 2

examines the history of art history as an academic discipline from the sixteenth century to the present through Warburg, Panofsky, Gombrich, Foucault and Derrida, the historiographical-methods counterpart to the shared Historiography of Media, Art, Design and Architecture component

examines key debates on modern art through the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies, the shared exhibition/museum-studies component every specialisation carries in year 2

studies how sculptures, masks and other forms of African visual expression embody cultural and social meaning and addresses the ethics and politics of colonial-era looting, museum acquisitions and repatriation, the heritage-and-conflict component shared by every specialisation

examines how humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural-minority and psychoanalytic perspectives affect reading and interpretation and has students apply selected perspectives to texts, the contested-reading and contested-images counterpart to the shared Contesting Images component

examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses and critically engages leading theories and debates about modernity, the contemporary-debates-in-culture counterpart to the shared Current Debates in Art and Culture component

provides a solid foundation in the study of film while introducing media more broadly, tracing the development of cinema and the elements of film form, and widens to television, streaming and digital platforms, the direct UCR counterpart to Film and Media History

explores the cultural and material significance of pre-digital media technologies such as cassette tapes, typewriters and early printed books and how they shaped the production and preservation of knowledge, extending the media-history core into the historical roots of media technology

examines social history and everyday life through American mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present, across television, film, podcasts and TikTok, analysing how digital and legacy storytelling technologies shape contemporary values, the direct UCR counterpart to Media Theory and Analysis

examines how environmental issues are represented and debated through visual and audiovisual media and how media shape the ways ecological problems are understood, felt and acted upon, a media-theory application of the core media-studies direction

examines how film, photography and music address systemic racism, critique the present and envision just futures, and whose stories are remembered or erased, applying media analysis to questions of representation and power

traces the development of the documentary form from its origins to the present and analyses non-fiction representations across documentary styles, genres and historical/social contexts, an advanced media-studies research course that provides the closest UCR counterpart to the specialisation's Research Seminar Media

studies the Greek and Roman roots of rhetoric and the craft of persuasive messages across tweets, advertising, protest speech and social media, the communication and creative/cultural-industries skill underlying the media direction's integrative concept
analyses the linguistic choices that create meaning in literary and non-fiction texts, a stylistic/analytical complement to the visual-culture-from-image-to-text core

examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested across texts, films, exhibitions, protest art and social media, a creative-industries and media-analysis application of contemporary cultural debate

examines persuasion strategies in local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions and their ethics, applying communication theory to the creative and cultural industries

examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation and artistic practice across poetry, performance and hybrid, sound-based or digitally mediated work, the closest UCR counterpart to the specialisation's Postmedium Condition: Contemporary Art and Media, which likewise studies contemporary art and media beyond a single medium

introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation across fiction, poetry, drama and film narration, the visual/textual-interpretation foundation that complements the core's visual-culture strand
explores how mythical narratives are transmitted across cultures and media, from epic poems to visual culture and theatrical performance, an integrative study of storytelling across text and image
studies how literary originals are translated to screen and offers instruction in film-analysis methodology, directly extending the media-studies core into film/text adaptation and narrative analysis

examines the painting, sculpture and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the trade, colonisation and cross-cultural exchange that shaped their production and meaning, the closest UCR counterpart to the specialisation's History of Media, Art, Design and Architecture: Early Modern

examines ancient craft production and how making objects shaped human and social identity from Çatalhöyük and Kush to classical Athens and Rome, the material-culture and historical-roots foundation of the art-history direction
explores the archaeology of community and democracy in early-democratic Greece, the ancient material and visual culture that grounds the western art-historical tradition

investigates how Athenian democracy was built and expressed in art, literature and architecture and traces its collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC, connecting ancient heritage to the heritage-and-conflict theme through the politics of its own commemoration

gives a chronological overview of the modern period (1815-2025), the political and social upheavals of industrial society, revolution and national self-determination, the historical-context foundation for studying art within its period

explores the histories and lived experience of gender across the nineteenth to twenty-first centuries, supplying the gender-historical lens increasingly central to contemporary art-historical interpretation

examines great powers, superpowers and hyperpowers and the ambiguous, contested history of empire, the imperial and colonial context in which much of the art-historical and heritage record was produced and collected

explores the causes, consequences and potential solutions to violent and nonviolent conflict across history, sociology and political science, directly extending the heritage-and-conflict theme into a dedicated conflict-studies course

trains sustained primary-source historical research through a case study of the 1809 Walcheren expedition, the research-seminar model of independent historical inquiry that provides the closest UCR counterpart to the specialisation's Research Seminar Art

examines the main theories of moral reasoning (virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism) and their application to practical questions, supplying the ethical framework that heritage and repatriation debates require

studies the legal, historical and philosophical dimensions of human rights, including treaties and case law, directly supporting the legal and ethical dimension of heritage, looting and repatriation debates

introduces the concepts, methods and theories sociology uses to understand the functioning of societies and global interconnections, a social-theoretical toolkit for analysing art's institutions and publics
trains qualitative research methodology, asking what counts as truth, reality and knowledge in enquiry, a qualitative-methods complement to the art-historical direction's research training

examines social-movement theory and environmental justice through case studies and feminist, anti-colonial and degrowth perspectives, extending the heritage-and-conflict theme into contemporary heritage and cultural activism
familiarises students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective, focusing on civil society, an advanced theoretical capstone for the art-history and heritage direction

offers a chronological overview of major literary texts from the epic of Gilgamesh to post-modernity that have for centuries inspired Western visual arts and theatre, a cultural-historical foundation for the art-history direction

alternatives.label: Media, Film & Communication
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by the full six-course UCR media-studies cluster (Introduction to Film & Media, Media Archaeology, From T.V. to TikTok, Media & the Environment, Media & Race, The Documentary) and the full five-course communication/rhetoric cluster, with literature and narrative-analysis courses (including Film & Text) in a supporting role and the shared visual-culture/heritage/philosophy spine underneath. The label names Media first, reflecting the specialisation actually reconstructed, and 'Film & Communication' names the curriculum's two other genuinely load-bearing strands; it does not claim design or architecture content that the completed 24-course curriculum does not contain.
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to VU's Media specialisation of the Media, Art, Design and Architecture bachelor: the complete UCR media-studies sequence (film and media history and theory, media archaeology, documentary, contemporary screen and platform culture, media and race, media and the environment) combined with rhetorical and persuasive communication, creative and experimental communication practice, literary and narrative analysis including film adaptation, and the shared visual-culture, research-methods, philosophy, heritage, exhibition, contested-images and contemporary-debates courses that VU itself teaches identically to every specialisation. It reproduces the specialisation's film/media-history, media-theory and postmedium/contemporary-art-and-media core as far as UCR allows and leaves VU's dedicated graphic-design, fashion, architecture and urban-planning content as an honest gap outside the Media route.
progression: No course used in this alternative carries a formal prerequisite in the enriched UCR course database, so sequencing is an open advisory choice rather than a hard constraint. Introductory (level-1) courses are concentrated in the first two years: Introduction to Film & Media, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Introduction to Literary Studies, Introduction to Western Art History and Media Archaeology open the programme, together with Research Methods & Statistics and Introduction to Western Philosophy in year 2, so that the media-studies, communication, literary-analysis and shared visual-culture/methods foundations are in place before advanced work. Advanced (level-3) courses are concentrated in years 2 and 3: Persuasive Communication, Media & Race, Film & Text and Modern Art & Modern Museums in semester 5, and The Documentary, Communicating the Climate Crisis, Creative Communication Laboratory and Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean in semester 6, so that the media/communication and historical-visual-culture strands both culminate late in the programme. Personal & Professional Development is scheduled in semester 2, within year 1. Every course is offered in its assigned semester.

alternatives.label: Art History & Heritage
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by the eight-course UCR cultural-heritage/art-history and archaeology cluster and a five-course history cluster, with law, philosophy, sociology and a literary-foundation course supplying the ethical, theoretical and cultural context that VU's Art specialisation gives to heritage, conflict and contemporary debate. The label names Art first, matching the specialisation reconstructed, and 'History & Heritage' names the curriculum's genuinely load-bearing historical and heritage-ethics strand; it does not claim the studio-practice or media content that the completed 24-course curriculum does not contain.
alternatives.concept: A response to VU's Art specialisation built around the historical, material and ethical study of art and cultural heritage: the full UCR cultural-heritage/art-history and archaeology cluster (Introduction to Western Art History, Introduction to World Archaeology, Greek Archaeology, Renaissance/African art and heritage, Modern Art & Modern Museums, Heritage & Ancient Democracy, Writing Art's Histories) combined with historical training (Modern History, Histories of Gender, History of Empires, the History Research Seminar), the legal, ethical and political study of heritage, conflict and human rights (Human Rights: Law & Philosophy, Ethics, Peace & Conflict), sociological theory and method (Introduction to Sociology, Qualitative Research Methodology, Social Movements & Environmental Justice, New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory) and a cultural-literary foundation (Great Literary Works), plus the same shared visual-culture, research-methods, philosophy, exhibition, heritage, contested-images and contemporary-debates courses used in the Media alternative. It reproduces VU's Art specialisation's grounding in the history and critical analysis of art across periods and cultures and its attention to museums, heritage and cultural conflict, while leaving VU's studio-adjacent contemporary-art-practice and media-specific content (which UCR does not offer) as an honest gap.
progression: No course used in this alternative carries a formal prerequisite in the enriched UCR course database. Introductory (level-1) courses open the programme: Introduction to Western Art History, Modern History, Introduction to World Archaeology, Introduction to Western Philosophy and Introduction to Sociology are concentrated in years 1 and 2, before Qualitative Research Methodology, History of Empires, Human Rights: Law & Philosophy and Histories of Gender extend method and historical range. Advanced (level-3) courses are concentrated in years 2 and 3: Heritage & Ancient Democracy in semester 1, Writing Art's Histories in semester 2, the History Research Seminar in semester 4, and Modern Art & Modern Museums, New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory and Peace & Conflict in semesters 5 and 6, so that the historiographical, research-seminar and advanced-theory work culminates after the historical and archaeological foundations are in place. Personal & Professional Development is scheduled in semester 1, within year 1. Every course is offered in its assigned semester.
alternatives.distinctness: The closest match applies VU's shared visual-culture, methods, philosophy, exhibition, heritage, contested-images and contemporary-debates courses to the Media specialisation's film, screen and communication core. This alternative keeps the same nine shared courses -- which represent components VU itself teaches identically across all four specialisations -- but replaces every one of the closest match's fifteen Media-specific courses (the full media-studies, communication/rhetoric and literary-narrative clusters, plus Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean) with fifteen courses evidenced by the Art specialisation instead: the remaining cultural-heritage/art-history and archaeology cluster, a five-course history cluster, heritage law, ethics and conflict studies, sociological theory and method, and a literary-foundation course. The two programmes therefore share only their nine common courses and differ in fifteen courses each (112.5 EC), far exceeding the 30-EC/4-course floor; the difference is a direct consequence of reconstructing a materially different formal specialisation rather than a cosmetic reshuffling of the same content.

blocks: Foundations of visual, material & academic culture

Both are the introductory course that develops the language and tools of visual/object analysis. VU's Image and Object Analysis teaches students to analyse objects, paintings, buildings, films and clips critically and historically; Introduction to Western Art History surveys the same skill through a chronological overview of Western art and the institutions that shape its reception.

Both are the programme's research-methods and techniques course. Onderzoekstechnieken introduces research skills for arts-and-culture study; Research Methods & Statistics teaches research design and descriptive/inferential statistics, a more quantitative emphasis than VU's own methods course.

Approaching Visual and Material Culture is a broader first-week orientation to analysing the form, operation and functioning of images, objects and spaces across all four fields. UCR's closest course, Introduction to Western Art History, is already matched to the more specific Image and Object Analysis, and no other UCR course offers the same general cross-disciplinary orientation, so no counterpart is claimed.

Academic Skills Arts and Culture develops discipline-specific academic writing and presentation skills for arts-and-culture study. UCR's academic-skills training is distributed across every course's written and oral assessment rather than concentrated in one dedicated skills course, so no single counterpart is claimed.
Academic English MKDA is a language-of-instruction requirement for students entering an otherwise Dutch-taught track. UCR is already fully English-medium, so no disciplinary counterpart is claimed.
Historical development of visual & material culture

Both examine early modern visual and material culture across a wide geography. History of Media, Art, Design and Architecture: Early Modern surveys the period generally across all four fields; Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean examines Renaissance Italian painting, sculpture and architecture and the trade and cross-cultural exchange that shaped it, a more geographically specific treatment of the same period.

Both survey a defined historical period as a chronological overview. European Cultural History covers Europe's cultural development; Modern History covers the modern period (1815-2025) with attention to the same industrial, political and revolutionary forces, from a general historical rather than an explicitly cultural angle. This row is available only in the Art alternative, which is organised around historical training; the Media alternative leaves it unmatched.

History of Media, Art, Design and Architecture: Modern is a period-specific survey of the modern era across all four fields. Modern Art & Modern Museums (matched to Exhibition Machines) and Modern History (matched to European Cultural History) are the closest available UCR courses and are already assigned elsewhere; no additional counterpart is claimed.

History of Media, Art, Design and Architecture: Contemporary surveys the most recent period across all four fields. No further UCR course beyond those already matched offers a dedicated contemporary-period survey of media, art, design and architecture together, so no counterpart is claimed.
The Netherlands TM is a thematic module situating the programme within a specifically Dutch context. UCR offers no dedicated course on the Netherlands, so no counterpart is claimed.
Shared exhibitions, philosophy, heritage & contemporary debate

Both concern how museums and exhibitions construct and present meaning. Exhibition Machines is VU's dedicated exhibition-studies course; Modern Art & Modern Museums examines the relationship between modern art and its presentation in museums, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.

Both examine how the disciplines of media, art, design and architecture have themselves been historically constructed. Historiography of Media, Art, Design and Architecture is VU's shared historiography course; Writing Art's Histories examines the history of art history as an academic discipline from the sixteenth century to the present through Warburg, Panofsky, Gombrich, Foucault and Derrida.

Both survey philosophy as a shared component of the curriculum. Philosophy CIS-L&S-MKDA is VU's shared philosophy course; Introduction to Western Philosophy surveys the discipline's central questions and methods from antiquity to the present.

Both address heritage and the conflicts surrounding it. World Heritage and Conflict is VU's dedicated component; African Art & Heritage studies west African visual/material culture and the ethics of colonial-era looting, museum acquisitions and the repatriation movement, a concrete case of contested heritage.

Urban Culture and Public Space is a dedicated urban-studies component. UCR's most closely related course, Spatial Planning, requires Sustainability Essentials II as a formal prerequisite and is not offered in any semester of the fixed Fall 2026 cohort, so it cannot be scheduled; no counterpart is claimed.
Study Trip Media and Design is a short-format international excursion specific to VU's own delivery. UCR has no equivalent short-format excursion course, so no counterpart is claimed.

Both examine how contested perspectives shape the reading of images and texts. Contesting Images is VU's shared component; Perspectives on Literary Meaning examines how humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural-minority and psychoanalytic perspectives affect reading and interpretation.

Both engage current debates in art and culture. Current Debates in Art and Culture is VU's shared component; Modern Sociology examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses and critically engages leading theories and debates about modernity.

The 30-EC year-3 elective period (a minor, individually chosen units of education, study abroad, or an internship plus electives) is genuinely open profiling space with no fixed content specified by VU. It is preserved as open space and not matched to any UCR course.

The BA-thesis MKDA is a 12-EC independent research project and colloquium. No scheduled UCR course is a thesis; UCR's standardised Optional independent research element is shown in this row instead, consistent with researchComponentId.

Both are the programme's dedicated film-history course. Film and Media History covers the Media specialisation's foundational film and media history; Introduction to Film & Media traces the development of cinema and the elements of film form before widening to media more broadly.

Both analyse contemporary media theoretically. Media Theory and Analysis is VU's dedicated theory course; From T.V. to TikTok examines mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present and how storytelling and representation shape contemporary understanding.

Both examine how media construct and mediate the environments people inhabit. Mediating Environments is VU's own Media-specialisation component on this theme; Media & the Environment examines how environmental issues are represented and debated through visual and audiovisual media.

Both study art and media beyond a single, stable medium. The Postmedium Condition: Contemporary Art and Media examines contemporary art's hybridity across media; Creative Communication Laboratory examines meaning produced through hybrid, experimental and digitally mediated communication across poetry, performance and sound, a comparable postmedium creative practice.

Both are advanced, research-oriented media-studies work late in the programme. Research Seminar Media is VU's specialisation-specific capstone seminar; The Documentary traces the development of a media form from its origins to the present through sustained research and analysis of primary examples, the closest UCR counterpart to a dedicated media-studies research seminar.

selection.assessment: The closest match owns the eleven generator-eligible rows that describe the programme's shared core and the Media graduation direction specifically: how images and objects shape our view of the world, what is real in contemporary visual culture, the historical roots of visual and material culture, the explicit integration of media, art, design and architecture, critical analysis of images/objects/spaces, media studies as a named graduation direction, film/television/game culture, digital media and changing storytelling technologies, visual culture from paintings to digital images, creative industries and cultural innovation, and researching art and culture independently. UCR can implement this core through its full media-studies, communication and literary-narrative offering together with the shared visual-culture, research-methods, philosophy, exhibition, heritage, contested-images and contemporary-debates courses VU itself teaches identically across every specialisation. The three remaining generator-eligible rows are each a single formal specialisation named as its own stable study direction and are assessed as three separate candidate directions rather than one omnibus 'other specialisations' bucket. Art history and contemporary art is evidenced by its own generator row and supported by the Creative Ecologies interest row; UCR's eight-course cultural-heritage/art-history and archaeology cluster, five-course history cluster, heritage law/ethics/conflict courses and sociological theory and method give it a materially different, defensible 24-course curriculum that shares only the nine components VU teaches identically to Media, so it is included as the second alternative. Design history and culture is evidenced by its own generator row and supported by the fashion/costume/material-culture interest row, but the enriched UCR course database contains no graphic-design, fashion-history or design-theory course; its only content-adjacent courses (Consumer Product Design, Marketing & Consumer Engagement and related BENENTR courses) teach commercial product design and marketing methodology, a different disciplinary orientation that would not be a defensible substitute for VU's historical/theoretical study of graphic design, fashion and applied arts, so this candidate is rejected as insufficient-evidence rather than manufactured from a weak substitute. Architecture, cities and spatial culture is evidenced by its own generator row; UCR offers no architecture, urban-design or landscape-architecture course, and its one plausible complementary course, Spatial Planning, is not offered in any semester of the fixed Fall 2026 cohort, so this candidate is rejected as not-feasible on both evidential and mechanical grounds. Because the next candidate considered in the programme's own official order (Media, Art, Design, Architecture) fails on insufficient evidence, production stops at two included alternatives.

notes.text: The Media, Art, Design and Architecture bachelor combines a formal Media graduation direction (film, television, internet and games) with a shared foundation in visual/material-culture analysis, historiography, exhibitions, heritage and philosophy. At UCR, students can approach media and visual culture through fields such as media studies, communication/rhetoric and literary/narrative analysis, and can approach art and heritage through cultural heritage, history, law, philosophy and sociology. UCR offers no single integrated programme spanning media, art, design and architecture together, and has no dedicated graphic-design, fashion-history or architecture/urban-design content at all, so these UCR alternatives offer related perspectives on two of the programme's four formal directions rather than reproducing the full Media, Art, Design and Architecture curriculum.
